commentary.bottom_line: Eighteen sources, including CHAI frameworks, NIST AI 600-1, and several commentaries, endorse IRB consultation before evaluating research-stage or non-cleared AI in human subjects, but no supplied study tests whether this practice protects patients. The recommendation rests on established research-ethics norms and expert consensus rather than on direct empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests IRB consultation for AI evaluation, and no study documents the hazard. Support comes from frameworks and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. The endorsements agree on the principle, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsements tie IRB review to regulatory status. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks teams to consult the IRB when an AI solution lacks FDA clearance. The NHS guide requires MHRA no-objection and REC clearance for un-marked device investigations. These statements describe existing research-oversight rules applied to AI, and no study measures compliance or its effects.

The CHAI guide frames the first step as deciding whether a deployment counts as human subjects research. That boundary between quality improvement and research may be hard to draw for AI tools already in live workflows. No supplied study measures how often systems misclassify projects or what IRB review adds in time or burden.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI evaluations conducted with and without IRB review on outcomes such as participant harm, consent quality, protocol deviations, or time to deployment. Studies are also needed on how institutions classify AI projects as research versus quality improvement and how consistently IRBs review AI-specific risks.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether IRB review of AI evaluations addresses consent comprehension or risks specific to these groups. The Uganda ethics-committee guide suggests that reviewer familiarity with AI varies across settings.
